evidence_quotes.quote: This study is a gap analysis between the WTP and the cost of service delivery for improved, formalized FS collection, operating in Kigali, Rwanda. Pit Vidura is a social enterprise that delivers formalized, improved pit latrine emptying and FS transport services to low-income households in informal settlements in Kigali.

In this paper, we construct a cost model of Pit Vidura’s formal pit emptying services, characterize the local market for sealing and emptying in informal settlements of Kigali, and then compare them both to estimates of willingness to pay (WTP) for Pit Vidura’s services.

While most governments provide heavy subsidies for storm water drainage, sewerage, and even wastewater treatment where it exists, the regulation, oversight, investment, and subsidy of FS management have been limited. Services are almost always provided by the private sector, and often by informal operators.

Each village was randomly assigned one type of coupon, and all of the participants in that village received the same coupon. Each coupon included a volumetric price for an individual empty, as well as a volumetric discount for a group empty

Cluster randomization of coupon prices allowed for us to create a statistical model of uptake, in order to model WTP while using a revealed preferences approach. We modeled two dependent variables while using logistic regression: (1) any request for emptying services; and, (2) any request for group emptying services.

Our study highlights the sizable gap that exists between the household willingness to pay and the cost of safe services. According to our estimates, only 15% of households currently choose to empty when their pits are full.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household access to, uptake of, and affordability of improved pit-latrine emptying and fecal sludge management (FSM) services in dense informal settlements of Kigali, Rwanda.
criterion_notes.c2: Fails Criterion 2 (E03 Wrong exposure). Plain wording: Primarily no (at most tangential background). Rather than studying a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or public governance factor, the study conducts an economic willingness-to-pay (WTP) experiment and firm-level operational truck-costing analysis for a private social enterprise (Pit Vidura). Mentions of fines for illegal dumping, forthcoming prohibitions on pit sealing, municipal tipping fees, and a hypothetical US$0.36/month FSM surcharge on solid waste bills are unanalysed background context, cost-accounting inputs, or Discussion-section policy proposals, not empirically evaluated exposures. Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Clearly no. Promotional market price coupons and group-coordination discounts offered by a private social enterprise, consumer stated preferences for service attributes (including volumetric vs. flat-fee pricing and branded/registered operators with worker PPE vs. informal laborers), operational truck scale (1-4 empties/day), and an observational control variable for whether tenants or landlords pay for pit maintenance do not constitute a rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, provider tenure/documentation requirements, regulated tariff or statutory cost-recovery rules, enforcement, or utility regulatory structure) directly governing service access.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary quantitative empirical evidence from a cluster-randomized revealed-preference price coupon trial (N = 1,167 households enrolled across 30 villages), a stated-preference discrete choice survey (N = 157 households and landlords), and operational cost accounting from Pit Vidura expense reports.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports outcomes directly relevant to sanitation service uptake/access and affordability, including household requests for improved pit-emptying services (individual and group empties), consumer willingness to pay per empty, and the affordability gap between household WTP and unit cost of safe service delivery.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (households in informal settlements of Kigali), exposures (randomized coupon prices and group discounts, household/pit covariates, DCE service attributes, and truck operational scale), outcomes (service requests, WTP, and unit cost per empty), and study design (cluster-randomized field trial, discrete choice experiment, and cost modeling) are all clearly specified.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is published in English.

study_design: Cluster-randomized revealed-preference field trial (price coupon experiment), stated-preference discrete choice survey, and operational cost modeling
population_and_sample: Households with latrines across 30 villages in 10 dense informal-settlement sectors of Kigali, Rwanda (N = 1,167 coupon-receiving households at baseline plus 12 neighbor households in revealed-preference models [N = 1,065 to 1,176 analyzed in regressions]; N = 157 households and landlords in follow-up stated-preference discrete choice survey; unit of analysis: household)
exposure: Randomly assigned promotional coupon volumetric prices (US$26.67 to US$93.33 per 1,200 L empty) and group-empty discounts (US$6.67 or US$13.33) offered by private social enterprise Pit Vidura; household covariates (pit fullness, whether household vs. landlord is responsible for pit maintenance costs); stated-preference service attributes (price, flat fee vs. volumetric pricing, branded/registered business with worker PPE vs. informal laborers, sludge treatment, distant disposal, response speed, pit fullness/group empty, sealing); and operational service scale (1 to 4 empties/day with rented flatbed vs. owned exhauster truck)
outcome: Household requests for Pit Vidura pit-latrine emptying services (any empty and group empty), stated-preference willingness to pay (US$ per empty), and unit operational/overhead cost per empty (cost-recovery/affordability gap)
rationale: Exclude as E03 (Wrong exposure). Although this empirical study examines household uptake and affordability of pit-latrine emptying services in informal settlements of Kigali (satisfying c1, c3, c4, c5, and c6), its evaluated exposures are market demand/price elasticity in a private social enterprise's promotional coupon experiment, consumer stated preferences for service attributes, and firm-level truck operational economies of scale ('demand aggregation'). It does not empirically examine a legal, administrative, regulatory, or governance rule-type mechanism governing service access under Criterion 2; statutory/regulatory mentions (illegal dumping fines, forthcoming bans on pit sealing, city tipping fees, and a hypothetical monthly FSM surcharge on solid waste bills) are unanalysed background or Discussion-level policy suggestions.
